name: Deepwater Horizon
volume_note: 3.19M bbl into the Gulf (US District Court, Phase Two findings, 2015)
summary: A fire and explosion occurred at approximately 11:00 PM CDT, April 20, 2010 on the Deepwater Horizon, a semisubmersible drilling platform, with more than 120 crew aboard. The Deepwater Horizon is located some 50 miles SE of the Mississippi Delta and contained an estimated 700,000 gallons of #2 Fuel Oil or Marine Diesel Fuel. (Related incidents: "Deepwater Horizon -- Florida Commands") Editor's Not...

response.quote: The highest priority areas identified along the coastal zone are the inlets.

response.action: Foam applied. The fire stopped for about 1 hr, then reignited. USCG measured tanks and reported 3-3.5 million gal lost or burned (reported).
response.quote: Status of the Mega Borg Fire aboard vessel stopped for approx. 1 hr. Foam applied but vessel reignited and continues to burn through vents.

response.action: RRT6 recommended to the OSC that an Alpha BioSea bioremediation experiment near the ship be allowed on a not-to-interfere basis (reported).
response.quote: the RRT concurred with the proposal, as presented, and voted to recommend to the OSC that the experiment be allowed on a not-to-interfere basis.

response.action: Controlled dispersant test on a slick 3-5 mi N of the tanker: 4 C-130 passes, about 800 gal. Pre/post water samples and fluorometry taken by CITATION (reported).
response.quote: Four passes were made by the C-130 across control area with approximately 800 gallons of dispersant dispensed.

response.action: Shoreline cleanup strategy meeting with OSC, state, City of Galveston and OOPS. Covered San Luis Pass and Bolivar Roads, plus state plans for volunteer tarball pickup (reported).
response.quote: The state also discussed its plans to use volunteers to do manual cleanup of tarballs.

response.action: Second foam application from 1000 to about 1345 put the fire out. Water spraying continued to cool the vessel, and personnel boarded at about 1530.
response.quote: At 1000 hours foam application was initiated and this continued until approximately 1345. After 1345, fire appeared to be out and water spraying was continued in an effort to lower vessel temperature.

response.action: Open-water bioremediation tests (AE BioSea Process) were run on June 15 and 18. Results were inconclusive.
response.quote: Bioremediation tests were conducted on June 15 and 18.

response.action: Trustees reviewed ELF's San Luis Pass protection plan. RRT agreed to boom selected beaches only once estuaries were protected and spare resources existed (reported).
response.quote: The RRT agreed to booming selected beaches under the provision that the estuaries where protected first and excess resources were available.

response.action: Chemistry showed that tarballs collected at Surfside Beach were not from the Mega Borg (reported).
response.quote: Confirmed that oil collected at that location was not from MEGA BORG

response.action: Mega Borg stopped leaking oil. Diver surveys found the hull intact and structurally sound.
response.quote: By June 16 the Mega Borg stopped leaking oil. Diver surveys of the vessel revealed that the hull of the Mega Borg was intact and structurally sound.

response.action: OSHA set cleanup training: manual crews need 4 hr formal training plus 20 hr on-the-job training. Skimming, mechanical crews and supervisors need 24 hr (reported).
response.quote: Contractors involved in manual clean up (using shovels, rakes, sorbent wipes) will be required to complete four hours of formal safety training and 20 hours OJT on scene.

response.action: SSC and Strike Team overflight to video the slick and locate recoverable oil for skimmers. Mexican skimmer arrived on scene (reported).
response.quote: Objectives of the flight were to video record areas of the slick and spot areas of "recoverable" for skimmers. The Mexican skimmer has arrived on scene.

response.action: NOAA preliminary beach survey before impact found 100-250 tarballs per 100 linear ft. Pits showed no buried oil (reported).
response.quote: The tarball count ranged from 100 to 250 tarballs per 100 linear feet of beach.

response.action: Dewatering of the Mega Borg continued, and the stern now had six feet of freeboard (reported).
response.quote: Since the commencement of the dewatering operation, the stern now has six feet of freeboard.

response.action: Sorbent boom placed across inlet cuts from High Island to Sabine Pass to protect marshes. Cleanup gear and sorbents staged on Bolivar Peninsula (reported).
response.quote: Sorbent boom is being placed across the inlet cuts from High Island to Sabine Pass to protect the marsh areas.

response.action: Volunteers collected and bagged stranded seaweed and debris from Sea Rim Park westward to reduce oily waste volume (reported).
response.quote: Volunteers are being directed to collect and bag stranded seaweed and debris from the shoreline in Sea Rim Park westward

response.action: Skimmers deactivated as recoverable oil fell to near-negligible amounts. Phase-down approved after an OSC overflight.
response.quote: Permission to begin the phase down was given following an overflight by the OSC to confirm the absence of any significant areas of "recoverable oil".

response.action: RRT6 committee recommended declining Sky Blue Chemicals' request to field-test Oil Spill Eater.
response.quote: The Committee recommended that Sky Blue Chemicals' request for field testing be declined.

response.action: Lightering of the cargo onto M/V JANUS began at 9:30 pm at 1000 tons/hour.
response.quote: Lightering of the vessel commenced at 9:30 pm last night and continues today.

response.action: Contractors in Galveston and Port Arthur on call, claiming 10-20 people within 2 hours. Sorbent boom along the refuge left 1-2 more weeks.
response.quote: Contractors claim they are able to respond to a call-out with 10-20 people within two hours.

response.action: Louisiana and contractors agreed to boom set sites east of Sabine Pass if oil is detected 1 mi east of the pass and 5 mi offshore.
response.quote: Contractors will deploy booms in specific locations identified by state reps if M/V MEGA BORG oil is detected 1 mile east of Sabine Pass and 5 miles offshore.

response.action: USCG sent a 41-footer from Port Arthur to check a sheen ribbon 10 mi south of the LA coast and sample it. No oil was found (reported).
response.quote: Coast Guard dispatched 41-footer from Port Arthur to investigate sheen and collect samples.

response.action: Beach crews picked up most Louisiana tarballs by hand. Lightly hit areas were left, on LDEQ advice that intervention could cause erosion damage.
response.quote: Beach crews manually picked up the majority of the tarballs. Some areas with a minimal amount of tarballs were not cleaned.

response.action: FOSC released the NOAA scientific support team. Galveston command post phones disconnected.
response.quote: The FOSC has released the NOAA scientific support team pending any further developments.

response.action: Remaining 809,500 bbl lightered off the Mega Borg using two small tankers. Completed July 27.
response.quote: The remaining 809,500 barrels of oil were lightered off the Mega Borg, using two small tankers. Lightering was completed on July 27.

totals.dispersant: Five sorties sprayed a total of 11,300 gallons of dispersant (Corexit 9527) (post 510206). Daily figures: about 4,000 gal on 6/10 (510206/510210), about 500 gal (510211), about 800 gal in the 6/14 test (510214)
totals.burned: Not quantified separately. 'An estimated 100,000 barrels ... was burned or released' (510205). USCG: '3 3.5 million gals. lost or burned' (510213). Up to 50% lost to evaporation or burned (510226)
totals.boom: 6,000 feet of 36-inch boom staged in Galveston (post 510206). Amount of sorbent boom deployed not stated
totals.shoreline_oiled: Small tarballs scattered over a distance of 18 miles (post 510226). Most on a five-mile stretch near Peveto Beach (post 510206)
totals.wildlife: Summary: no reports of oiled wildlife (510206); but 2007 photo posts show oiled sea turtles (517525)

name: Burmah Agate
volume_note: 10.7M gal total: ~2.6M gal released to the environment + ~7.8M gal burned on board (IncidentNews); 2,100 bbl reached shore
commodity: Nigerian Crude, blended crude (high naphtha content)
summary: On the morning of November 1, 1979, the Burmah Agate and the Mimosa collided at the entrance to Galveston Harbor. The Mimosa struck the Burmah Agate on its starboard side, tearing an 8 by 15 foot hole in the hull near Cargo Tank No. 5. An explosion occurred upon impact, and the leaking oil ignited. The USCG immediately dispatched the Coast Guard Cutter Valiant to begin search and rescue operations...
release: tanker collision and fire off Galveston entrance

evolution.note: Oil came ashore at the Galveston Jetties and East Beach.
evolution.quote: Oil came ashore on November 5 at Galveston Jetties and East Beach, and cleanup began immediately.

evolution.note: Oil reached the Matagorda Peninsula.
evolution.quote: Oil impacted the Matagorda Peninsula on November 6.

evolution.note: Six barrels hit 437 yards of marsh and sand beach around Smith Point (the only inland impact) and five areas on Galveston Island.
evolution.quote: On November 9, six barrels of oil impacted 437 yards of marshes and sand beaches around Smith Point and five areas on Galveston Island.

evolution.note: Slick of sheen and mousse in windrows extended 8.5 miles WSW of the tanker.
evolution.quote: By November 12, a slick composed of sheen and mousse in windrows extended 8.5 miles WSW of the tanker.

evolution.note: Small tarballs reached Padre Island near Mansfield Pass (~8 bbl ashore, not cleaned).
evolution.quote: Oil in the form of small tarballs impacted Padre Island near Mansfield Pass on November 13.

evolution.note: Heavy oil on Galveston beaches; heaviest impacts near Jamaica Beach Nov 19-21.
evolution.quote: Heavy concentrations of oil impacted Galveston beaches on November 18. The heaviest impacts of oil occurred near Jamaica Beach November 19-21.

evolution.note: Streamers observed near Bolivar Peninsula.
evolution.quote: Streamers were observed near Bolivar Peninsula on November 27.

evolution.note: A 19-mile slick extended SSW of the tanker; seasonal winds kept most oil offshore.
evolution.quote: by December 7, a 19 mile long slick extended to the SSW of the tanker.

response.action: USCGC Valiant dispatched for search and rescue; owners took responsibility and hired Clean Water, Inc. (cleanup) and Smit International (firefighting/salvage).
response.quote: They contracted Clean Water, Inc. for cleanup operations, and Smit International Inc. to fight fires on the Burmah Agate, and to assist in salvage.

response.action: Galveston shipping lanes closed both ways for a short time (again Nov 5 while the Mimosa was towed in).
response.quote: The shipping lanes into Galveston were closed in both directions for a short time on the first day of the incident, and again on November 5

response.action: USCG Gulf Strike Team arrived with 612 ft of OWOCRS and two ADAPTS pumps.
response.quote: On November 2, the GST arrived with 612 feet of Open Water Oil Containment and Recovery System (OWOCRS)

response.action: Strike Team deployed boom astern of the burning tanker overnight; kinks, no boom lights and a fouled propeller.
response.quote: GST personnel worked through the night and into the morning of November 3 to deploy a boom astern of the tanker.

response.action: Cleanup began immediately when oil reached Galveston Jetties and East Beach.
response.quote: Oil came ashore on November 5 at Galveston Jetties and East Beach, and cleanup began immediately.

response.action: After new explosions opened more tanks, OSC called in the Navy Supervisor of Salvage for booms, skimmers and operators.
response.quote: contacted the U.S. Navy Supervisor of Salvage (NAVSUPSALV) to bring in booms and skimmers with personnel to operate them.

response.action: 2,000 ft of Goodyear boom north of the tanker to protect Galveston Channel and Bolivar Peninsula; 4,000 ft to close San Luis Pass.
response.quote: On November 10, 2,000 feet of Goodyear boom was deployed north of the Burmah Agate to protect the Galveston Channel and Bolivar Peninsula.

response.action: Marco Class V skimmer deployed behind the boom where oil was entraining underneath.
response.quote: On November 11, a Marco Class V skimmer was deployed to back up the boom under which oil had entrained.

response.action: Two OWOCRS skimming barriers deployed.
response.quote: On November 13, two OWOCRS were deployed.

response.action: Burning oil from tank explosions set the booms on fire (again on Nov 14); 4,000 ft of Goodyear boom and one OWOCRS were lost to fire.
response.quote: The boom caught fire again on November 14.

response.action: Vessels with outrigger-mounted Marco and Lockheed skimmers began skimming.
response.quote: came on scene and began skimming operations.

response.action: 400 people cleaning beaches; front-end loaders took too much sand, so vacuum trucks were used.
response.quote: By November 21, there were 400 people cleaning the beaches.

response.action: Weather stopped firefighting and skimmers (Nov 22) and all cleanup (Nov 28-29); OWOCRS failed in currents of 0.75-1 knot.
response.quote: Oil began to entrain under the OWOCRS when the current reached .75 knots, and once the current reached 1 knot the OWOCRS were totally useless.

response.action: Beach cleanup complete; marshes at Smith Point left uncleaned to avoid more damage.
response.quote: Cleanup of beaches was complete by November 27.

response.action: Anchored foreign vessel dragged anchor and carried away the Goodyear booms; redeployed next day.
response.quote: On December 17 a foreign vessel anchored near the Burmah Agate and carried away the Goodyear booms as it dragged anchor.

response.action: Fire extinguished; 4,000 ft of boom and OWOCRS deployed ahead of lightering.
response.quote: On January 8, the fire was put out, and deployment of 4000 feet of Goodyear boom and OWOCRS began in anticipation of lightering efforts.

response.action: Lightering Jan 17-Feb 3 recovered ~160,000 bbl of crude (38% of the cargo).
response.quote: Approximately 160,000 barrels of crude oil were recovered by lightering operations.

response.action: Tanker towed to Brownsville for scrapping. Of oil not lightered: ~48% burned, 12% dispersed offshore, 1.7% skimmed, 0.5% on beaches.
response.quote: Of the remaining oil, an estimated 1.7 per cent was picked up by skimmers, .5 per cent impacted beaches, 48 per cent burned, and 12 per cent dispersed offshore.

response_summary.outcome: Fire burned until 1980-01-08 and consumed most of the spilled oil; booms and skimmers worked poorly in winter seas and currents; Galveston beaches cleaned by 11/27; remaining cargo lightered.

totals.recovered: ~160,000 bbl lightered (38% of cargo); skimmers ~1.7% of the remaining oil
totals.burned: ~48% of the oil not lightered burned on/near the ship
totals.boom: 612 ft OWOCRS (11/2), 2,000 + 4,000 ft Goodyear boom (11/10), 4,000 ft lost to fire
totals.shoreline_oiled: 2,100 bbl reached beaches and marshes (Galveston, San Jose Island, Padre Island, Bolivar, Smith Point)

no wildlife counts

name: Ixtoc I
summary: On June 3, 1979, the 2 mile deep exploratory well, IXTOC I, blew out in the Bahia de Campeche, 600 miles south of Texas in the Gulf of Mexico. The water depth at the wellhead site is about 50 m (164 feet). The IXTOC I was being drilled by the SEDCO 135, a semi-submersible platform on lease to Petroleos Mexicanos (PEMEX). A loss of drilling mud circulation caused the blowout to occur. The oil and g...
release: shallow-water well blowout (50 m), Bahia de Campeche

evolution.note: Flow of ~30,000 bbl/day; prevailing northerly currents in the western Gulf carried oil toward the US; a 60 x 70 mile sheen patch moved toward Texas.
evolution.quote: Prevailing northerly currents in the western Gulf of Mexico carried spilled oil toward the U.S.

evolution.note: Tarballs hit a 17-mile stretch of Texas beach (about 600 miles from the well).
evolution.quote: On August 6, 1979, tarballs from the spill impacted a 17 mile stretch of Texas beach.

evolution.note: Mousse came ashore north of Port Mansfield Channel (again Aug 18).
evolution.quote: Mousse patches impacted the shoreline north of Port Mansfield Channel on August 15 and again on August 18.

evolution.note: Mousse ashore south of Aransas Pass; by Aug 26 most of North Padre Island moderately oiled.
evolution.quote: On August 24, mousse impacted shoreline south of Aransas Pass. By August 26, most of North Padre Island was covered with moderate amounts of oil.

evolution.note: When Hurricane Henri grounded the spray planes in late September, oil stranded on the western Yucatan shoreline; some had stranded north of Tampico.
evolution.quote: At that time oil stranded on the western Yucatan shoreline

evolution.note: All of the south Texas coast had been oiled.
evolution.quote: As of September 1, all of the south Texas coast had been impacted by oil.

evolution.note: Storm (Sep 13-15) removed most beached oil and washed oil over the barrier islands; afterwards only tarmats seen.
evolution.quote: A storm lasting from September 13-15 removed the majority of the oil.

response.action: PEMEX contracted Conair to spray Corexit 9527 from aircraft: 493 missions treated 1,100 sq mi of slick (June-Dec).
response.quote: A total of 493 aerial missions were flown, treating 1,100 square miles of oil slick.

response.action: Norwegian experts brought in skimming equipment and containment boom for cleanup in Mexico.
response.quote: Norwegian experts were contracted to bring in skimming equipment and containment booms, and to begin cleanup of the spilled oil.

response.action: Two months of warning led to the first Environmental Sensitivity Index (ESI) maps of the Texas coast; booms placed using them.
response.quote: This led to a mapping project which resulted in the first Environmental Sensitivity Index (ESI)

response.action: PEMEX hired blowout experts (Red Adair, Martech, Daivaz); divers activated the BOP but had to reopen it as valves began to rupture.
response.quote: Divers were eventually able to reach and activate the BOP, but the pressure of the oil and gas caused the valves to begin rupturing.

response.action: Pumping mud into the well cut flow from ~30,000 to ~20,000 bbl/day.
response.quote: In July 1979 the pumping of mud into the well reduced the flow to 20,000 barrels per day

response.action: Nearly 100,000 steel, iron and lead balls pumped into the well cut flow to ~10,000 bbl/day.
response.quote: early in August the pumping of nearly 100,000 steel, iron, and lead balls into the well reduced the flow to 10,000 barrels per day.

response.action: Texas: booms and skimmers protected the inlets first (Brazos-Santiago Pass, Port Mansfield Channel, Aransas Pass; Cedar Bayou sealed with sand).
response.quote: Efforts were concentrated on the Brazos-Santiago Pass, Port Mansfield Channel, Aransas Pass, and Cedar Bayou

response.action: Sensitive barrier-island beaches cleaned daily by hand (rakes, shovels) rather than heavy equipment; >10,000 cu yd oiled material removed.
response.quote: Laborers used rakes and shovels to clean beaches rather than heavier equipment which removed too much sand.

response.action: USFWS began training volunteers for oiled birds, beach patrols on South Padre; cleaning stations on Mustang and South Padre Islands. 1,421 oiled birds recovered.
response.quote: On August 8, the United States Fish and Wildlife Service (USFWS) began training volunteers for the handling of oiled birds

response.action: Well capped after ~290 days, after mud, steel/lead balls and two relief wells. PEMEX claimed half the oil burned at the surface, a third evaporated.
response.quote: PEMEX claimed that half of the released oil burned when it reached the surface, a third of it evaporated, and the rest was contained or dispersed.

response_summary.outcome: ~3 million bbl over 290 days. Mexico relied on aerial dispersants and relief wells; Texas protected inlets with booms/skimmers and hand-cleaned beaches. A September storm cleared most beached oil.

totals.shoreline_oiled: 71,500 bbl on 162 miles of US beaches; >10,000 cu yd oiled material removed
